A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FastPD research, with matching algorithms, propositions and proofs. Their main text, figures, tables and appendices provide sufficient material for a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations of SHAP estimation error, runtime and functional-component recovery in Figures 1–4 and Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 reports original simulations, additional correlation experiments, regression and classification benchmarks, and an Adult dataset case study, including extensive appendix results.

M1.justification: FastPD retains the same tree augmentation, empirical leaf probabilities, evaluation traversal and caching procedure. Revised pseudocode makes inputs, outputs and previously described caching more explicit; it does not establish a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic Gaussian regression settings only. v2 adds 35 OpenML-CTR23 regression datasets and 61 OpenML-CC18 classification datasets, including a dedicated Adult analysis. Additional simulations cover different correlations and eight-covariate inputs.

E2.justification: The reported runtime comparison expands from FastPD and TreeSHAP-int in v1 Figure 3 to five methods in v2 Figure 4, adding VanillaPD, Zern et al. (2023) and TreeSHAP-path. Zern was previously discussed theoretically but not included in the runtime results.

E3.justification: New benchmark protocols introduce 100-setting cross-validation searches, component-importance and relative-discrepancy metrics, and multiclass score aggregation; Adult uses a separate 25-trial tuning protocol. The illustrative SHAP plots also change from selecting FastPD's median-MSE run for both methods to selecting each method's own median run. Existing main simulation tuning was already documented in v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds correlation sensitivity analyses in Figures 7–10, including uncorrelated and strongly correlated inputs, eight-covariate experiments, and comparisons between fitted-model and ground-truth components. The Adult age–relationship interaction case study adds an application-level examination of conflicting explanations. These analyses are absent from v1.

E5.justification: v1's runtime figure reports medians over 100 runs and mentions 95% confidence bands; v2 reports means over 100 runs and drops that confidence-band statement. New Figure 10 specifies 150 runs. This does not establish an increase in repetitions for the retained main experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive attribution results: discrepancies exceeding 30% occur in 33, 18 and 9 of 96 datasets for Friedman-path, FastPD-50 and FastPD-100, respectively, matching the non-intercept appendix entries. It also adds correlation findings and replaces runtime results, reporting 1.26 seconds for both FastPD and Zern at 8000 points. Changed implementation descriptions, timed outputs and summary statistics preclude treating the runtime revision as a clean same-setting speedup.

T1.justification: The two propositions and Appendix B proofs are retained. v2 introduces the component-importance definition in Equation (10). Its rewritten SHAP definition in Equation (5) omits the 1/d normalization required for inverse-binomial weights, unlike v1's factorial formula and the retained two-feature proof. This introduces a localized mathematical error.

C1.justification: The central claims remain consistent estimation of arbitrary PD functions, linear sample-size scaling for moderately deep trees, recovery of SHAP and functional decompositions, and possible inconsistency of path-dependent TreeSHAP. The expanded experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's existing memory and extrapolation caveats, v2 explains finite-sample TreeSHAP-path error through reduced effective sample size and interprets high-correlation failures to recover ground truth. It adds guidance on checking background-sample adequacy, truncating higher-order interactions, and supplementing exploratory ground-truth explanations with semiparametric or doubly robust estimators.

D1.justification: v2 documents Rcpp bindings, pltreeshap and the VanillaPD implementation, plus Adult preprocessing, selected hyperparameters, benchmark configurations and multiclass explanation targets. Code-access instructions change from the explicit simulation-repository URL to the existing glex package and a named attached codeforsimulations repository; this does not establish newly available code.

R1.justification: Targeted additions include FastSHAP, further functional-ANOVA connections, and references supporting doubly robust estimation and ALE. SHAP-definition attribution changes from Lundberg and Lee (2017) to Strumbelj and Kononenko (2010). These broaden context without fundamentally changing FastPD's positioning relative to existing tree-based methods.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the introduction and algorithm exposition, reorganizes motivation and complexity explanations, and converts the simulation paragraphs into numbered subsections. Separate real-data sections and appendix material reshape the narrative, beyond merely adding result entries.

P2.justification: v2 adds an augmentation diagram, an Adult interaction figure, four supplementary sensitivity figures and extensive color-coded benchmark tables. The runtime figure changes from a two-method linear-scale plot to a five-method log-log plot with slopes and numerical summaries. Algorithms and several existing plots are also reformatted.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's validation through real-data attribution comparisons, runtime evaluation against the efficient Zern method, and sensitivity analyses exposing model-versus-ground-truth limitations. These substantially strengthen the evidence for practical applicability and clarify its boundaries. The gains are tempered by the missing SHAP normalization in Equation (5), inconsistent simulation references in Appendix A, and reduced runtime uncertainty reporting, but the retained FastPD derivation and proofs together with the broader validation support a substantial net improvement.
